title: Loads and load combinations
summary: Two things carry this subchapter: the partial safety factors and the load combinations of IS 456 Table 18, and the seismic coefficient of NBC 105. Memorise the combinations exactly — including the 0.9DL case, which exists to check uplift and overturning and is the one most often forgotten. Understand why the concrete factor (1.5) exceeds the steel factor (1.15), and why the response reduction factor R rewards ductility, because both reasons are examinable in themselves.

sections.heading: Design philosophies
sections.body:
Three philosophies have governed structural design in turn, and questions often ask which characteristic belongs to which:

| Method | Basis | Character |
|---|---|---|
| **Working stress method (WSM)** | Elastic theory; a single **factor of safety** applied to the material strength | Simple, but wasteful — it keeps stresses so low that the material's real reserve is never used, and it says nothing about the actual margin against collapse |
| **Ultimate load method** | Collapse load ÷ a **load factor** | Addresses strength but ignores **serviceability** — deflection and cracking are unchecked |
| **Limit state method (LSM)** | **Separate partial factors** on loads and on materials, checked against **several limit states** | The current basis of IS 456, IS 800 and NBC 105 |

**Why limit state design superseded the others.** The two earlier methods each applied a single factor to one side of the problem. WSM factored the **material** and hoped the loads were as assumed; the ultimate load method factored the **load** and hoped the material was as assumed. Neither reflects the fact that **loads and material strengths are uncertain in different ways and to different degrees** — a dead load is known within a few percent, an earthquake load within a factor of two; factory-rolled steel is far more consistent than site-made concrete.

Limit state design assigns a **partial factor to each source of uncertainty separately**, which is why it can be both safer and more economical than either predecessor.

**The limit states**, in two groups:

| Group | Limit states | Loads used |
|---|---|---|
| **Collapse (ultimate)** | Flexure, shear, torsion, compression, bond, overturning, sliding, buckling, fatigue | **FACTORED** loads; **reduced** material strengths |
| **Serviceability** | **Deflection**, **cracking**, vibration, durability | **Unfactored (characteristic)** loads, γ = 1.0 |

That difference in load factors between the two groups is itself a standard question. Serviceability uses unfactored loads because the question being asked is *what will actually happen in service*, not *what is the worst credible case*.

**Crack width limits (IS 456):**

| Exposure | Limit |
|---|---|
| **Normal** | **0.3 mm** |
| **Aggressive / severe** | **0.2 mm** |
| Where appearance is critical | 0.1 mm |

**Characteristic values.** The definitions are symmetric, and both take the unfavourable 5% tail:

> **Characteristic strength** — the value below which **not more than 5%** of test results are expected to fall.
> **Characteristic load** — the value with a **5% chance of being exceeded** during the structure's life.

That symmetry is what makes limit state design a coherent probabilistic framework rather than a collection of arbitrary factors.

sections.heading: Partial safety factors and load combinations
sections.body:
**Partial safety factors for materials (IS 456 cl. 36.4.2):**

> **γ_concrete = 1.5**   →   design strength **0.67 f_ck / 1.5 = 0.446 f_ck**
> **γ_steel = 1.15**   →   design strength **f_y / 1.15 = 0.87 f_y**

**Why concrete's factor is higher.** Steel is a **factory-manufactured product** of tightly controlled composition and consistent properties, tested batch by batch. Concrete is **made on site** from natural materials, batched, mixed, placed, compacted and cured under site conditions, so its in-place strength is far more variable than a cube test suggests. The larger factor buys back that extra uncertainty.

The **0.67** in the concrete expression is a separate allowance: it converts the cube strength to the strength of concrete in a **flexural compression zone under sustained load**, which is lower than the short-term cube value.

IS 800:2007 uses the same idea for steel with two factors:

> **γ_m0 = 1.10** for yielding and buckling
> **γ_m1 = 1.25** for **ultimate (rupture)**

Rupture takes the larger factor because it is a **brittle** failure mode with no warning, whereas yielding is ductile and gives visible deformation first. That reasoning — **larger factors for brittle modes** — recurs throughout the codes.

**Load combinations (IS 456 Table 18)** — these must be known exactly:

| Combination | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **1.5 (DL + LL)** | The basic gravity case |
| **1.2 (DL + LL ± WL/EL)** | Gravity with lateral load |
| **1.5 (DL ± WL/EL)** | Lateral load without live load |
| **0.9 DL ± 1.5 WL/EL** | **Uplift and overturning** |

**The 0.9DL case is the one most often forgotten**, and it exists for a specific reason: where dead load is a **stabilising** action, an *over*estimate of it is unsafe. So its favourable value is **reduced** to 0.9, while the destabilising lateral load is factored **up** to 1.5. Any check on **overturning, sliding, uplift of a footing, or tension in a holding-down bolt** must use this combination, and using 1.5DL there would conceal the problem entirely.

Note also that the combination with lateral load uses **1.2** rather than 1.5 on the gravity loads. The reason is probabilistic: it is very unlikely that the maximum dead, live **and** wind or earthquake loads occur simultaneously, so requiring each at its full factored value at once would be unreasonably conservative.

**For serviceability**, the combinations use γ = 1.0 on DL and LL, and **0.8** on LL when combined with wind or earthquake.

**A worked illustration of why the factors matter.** A slab with DL = 6 kN/m² and LL = 3 kN/m²: the factored design load is 1.5(6 + 3) = **13.5 kN/m²**, and the section is proportioned so that its design capacity — computed with 0.446 f_ck and 0.87 f_y — just carries it. The overall margin against collapse is therefore roughly 1.5 × 1.5 ≈ 2.25 on the concrete and 1.5 × 1.15 ≈ 1.7 on the steel, without either being applied twice.

sections.heading: Dead and imposed loads
sections.body:
**Dead load** is the self-weight of the permanent construction, computed from the dimensions and the unit weights of **IS 875 Part 1**:

| Material | Unit weight (kN/m³) |
|---|---|
| **Reinforced concrete** | **25** |
| Plain concrete | 24 |
| **Brick masonry** | **19 – 20** |
| Stone masonry | 24 – 26 |
| **Steel** | **78.5** |
| Cement mortar / plaster | 20 – 21 |
| Timber | 6 – 9 |
| **Water** | **9.81** |
| Soil (bulk) | 16 – 20 |

The **25 kN/m³ for RCC** is the most-used number in structural design, and floor finishes are commonly allowed as an additional **1 to 1.5 kN/m²** with partitions at **1 to 2 kN/m²** where their position is not fixed.

**Imposed (live) load — IS 875 Part 2:**

| Occupancy | Load (kN/m²) |
|---|---|
| **Residential — rooms** | **2.0** |
| Residential — corridors, stairs, balconies | 3.0 |
| **Office — rooms** | **2.5** (4.0 where filing or storage) |
| Office — corridors and stairs | 4.0 |
| **Classroom** | **3.0** |
| **Assembly with fixed seats** | **4.0** |
| **Assembly without fixed seats** | **5.0** |
| Shops, warehouses (light) | 4.0 – 5.0 |
| **Flat roof, accessible** | **1.5** |
| Flat roof, inaccessible | 0.75 |
| Sloping roof (> 10°) | 0.75 reducing with slope |

**Live load reduction on columns.** The probability that **every** floor carries its full imposed load simultaneously falls as the number of floors increases, so IS 875 permits a reduction on the cumulative load carried by a column:

| Floors carried | Reduction |
|---|---|
| 1 (roof) | 0% |
| 2 | 10% |
| 3 | 20% |
| 4 | 30% |
| 5 – 10 | 40% |
| **Over 10** | **50%** |

No reduction is permitted where the imposed load exceeds 5 kN/m² (warehouses, plant rooms), because there the load is more nearly permanent.

**Pattern loading.** For a **continuous** beam or slab, the worst moment at a section does not occur with every span loaded. The maximum **sagging** moment in a span occurs with that span and alternate spans loaded; the maximum **hogging** moment at a support with the two adjacent spans loaded. IS 456 therefore requires the arrangements:

- **All spans** carrying full DL + LL
- **Alternate spans** carrying full DL + LL, the others DL only
- **Two adjacent spans** carrying full DL + LL, the others DL only

The reason is exactly the influence-line argument: a UDL should cover the whole **positive** region of the influence line for the effect being maximised, and no more.

**Other loads** to be considered where relevant: **earth pressure**, **water and hydrostatic pressure**, **temperature** effects, **shrinkage and creep**, **settlement**, **snow load** (IS 875 Part 4 — significant in Nepal's high hills), **erection loads**, **impact and vibration**, and **accidental actions**.

sections.heading: Wind and seismic loads
sections.body:
**Wind load — IS 875 Part 3:**

> **Design wind speed V_z = V_b · k₁ · k₂ · k₃**
> **Design wind pressure p_z = 0.6 V_z²**  (N/m², V_z in m/s)

| Factor | Accounts for |
|---|---|
| **V_b** basic wind speed | Regional 3-second gust, 50-year return period |
| **k₁** risk coefficient | The structure's **design life and importance** |
| **k₂** terrain, height and structure size | Roughness of the surroundings and height above ground |
| **k₃** topography factor | Hills, ridges, escarpments — local speed-up |

The **force** on a surface is then **F = (C_pe − C_pi) A p_z**, using external and internal pressure coefficients.

**The k₃ topography factor matters greatly in Nepal**, where structures on ridges and hilltops experience substantially accelerated wind. A building sited on a ridge crest can see a wind pressure well above the value for flat terrain at the same location.

**Wind or earthquake — which governs?** The comparison is worth understanding because it decides where design effort goes:

| Governs for | Because |
|---|---|
| **Wind** — tall, light, large-surface structures | Wind force is proportional to **exposed AREA** |
| **Earthquake** — heavy, massive structures | Seismic force is proportional to **MASS** |

So a light steel-framed industrial shed with large cladding area is usually wind-governed, while a multi-storey reinforced concrete building in Nepal is almost always **earthquake-governed**.

**Seismic load — NBC 105:2020 (Nepal) and IS 1893:**

> **Design horizontal base shear V_B = C_d(T) · W**

In the IS 1893 form the coefficient is written

> **A_h = (Z/2) · (I/R) · (S_a/g)**

| Term | Represents |
|---|---|
| **Z** zone factor | The **seismic hazard** at the site |
| **I** importance factor | The **consequence** of failure — hospitals, schools and emergency facilities take a higher value |
| **R** response reduction factor | The structure's **ductility and energy absorption** |
| **S_a/g** spectral acceleration | The **dynamic response** at the building's natural period T |

**The response reduction factor R is the most instructive term.** It appears in the **denominator**, so a **higher R gives a LOWER design force**:

| System | R (IS 1893) |
|---|---|
| Ordinary RC moment-resisting frame | **3.0** |
| **Special (ductile) RC moment-resisting frame** | **5.0** |
| Ordinary shear wall | 3.0 |
| Ductile shear wall with SMRF | 5.0 |
| Unreinforced masonry | 1.5 |

A ductile frame is therefore designed for a force **40% lower** than an ordinary one — a very large economic difference. But the reduction is **earned**, not given: it is permitted **only if the detailing rules of IS 13920 are followed**, because R represents the structure's capacity to **deform inelastically without collapsing**. Claiming R = 5 and then detailing as an ordinary frame is not a conservative approximation; it is a design that will fail in the manner the reduction assumed it would not.

That is the central idea of seismic design, and it explains why the code's **detailing** provisions carry the same weight as its calculations.

**Natural period.** The base shear depends on **T**, estimated empirically:

> **T = 0.075 h^{0.75}** for a bare RC moment-resisting frame
> **T = 0.09 h/√d** for a frame with brick infill

**Distribution of base shear** up the height is roughly parabolic:

> **Q_i = V_B · (W_i h_i²) / Σ(W_j h_j²)**

so upper storeys attract disproportionately more force — which is why lightweight upper floors and roofs are beneficial and why heavy water tanks on roofs are a liability.

**Methods of analysis:**

| Method | Applies to |
|---|---|
| **Equivalent static (seismic coefficient)** | Regular buildings up to a height limit |
| **Response spectrum (modal)** | Taller or **irregular** buildings |
| Time history | Important or unusual structures |

**Irregularities** that trigger dynamic analysis and that must be avoided at the planning stage: **vertical irregularity** (a **soft or weak storey** — the open ground floor, which was a major cause of collapse in 2015), **mass irregularity**, **plan irregularity** and **re-entrant corners** (an L or T plan), **torsional irregularity** where the centre of mass and centre of stiffness do not coincide, and **discontinuity in the load path**.

**Nepal's code context.** **NBC 105:2020** replaced the 1994 edition, introducing modern spectral shapes, **ductility classes**, and explicit requirements reflecting the lessons of the **2015 Gorkha earthquake**. For load-bearing masonry, **NBC 202** gives Mandatory Rules of Thumb — horizontal bands at plinth, sill, lintel and roof level with vertical bars at corners and openings — which tie the walls into a box so they act together rather than as independent panels.

formulas.label: Partial safety factors for materials
formulas.note: Concrete's is higher because it is made on site; steel is a consistent factory product.

formulas.label: Load combinations (IS 456 Table 18)
formulas.note: The 0.9DL case checks UPLIFT and OVERTURNING, where dead load is stabilising and must be reduced.

formulas.label: Steel partial factors (IS 800)
formulas.note: Rupture takes the larger factor because it is a brittle mode with no warning.

formulas.label: Wind pressure
formulas.expression: V_z = V_b k₁ k₂ k₃ ;   p_z = 0.6 V_z²  (N/m²) ;   F = (C_pe − C_pi) A p_z
formulas.note: k₃ (topography) is significant in Nepal — ridges and hilltops accelerate the wind.

formulas.label: Seismic base shear
formulas.note: R is in the DENOMINATOR: higher ductility earns a lower design force, but only with IS 13920 detailing.

formulas.label: Fundamental natural period
formulas.expression: T = 0.075 h^{0.75} (bare RC frame) ;   T = 0.09 h/√d (frame with brick infill)
formulas.note: The spectral acceleration S_a/g is read at this period.

formulas.label: Vertical distribution of base shear
formulas.note: Roughly parabolic, so upper storeys attract disproportionate force — keep roof masses light.

formulas.label: Live load reduction on columns
formulas.expression: 10% per floor carried, to a maximum of 50% for more than 10 floors
formulas.note: No reduction where the imposed load exceeds 5 kN/m², since it is then nearly permanent.
